## Chapter 28: The Hog's Head

"We're shut," said the barman.

He did not look up. He was behind the bar at the far end of the one small room, wiping a glass with a cloth that was very much dirtier than the glass, and the room was dark, lit by two stubs of candle on tables nobody was sitting at, and it smelled strongly of goats.

"The door was open," said Evelyn.

"Door's always open. Doesn't mean I'm not shut." He put the glass down and picked up another one. "What do two Hufflepuff second-years want in my pub at midnight? Besides a hiding."

Harry read him.

He had been reading him through the door, and it was the same now, only closer. The man was old. He was very old, and he was tall and thin, with long grey hair and a long grey beard that both wanted cutting, and he was wearing something that might once have been a robe and was now mostly patches. And he was loud.

He was not loud the way Hagrid was loud, or Aunt Marge. He was loud the way a cellar full of something is loud, from underneath, through the floor. Everything in him had been held down for so long that it had gone hard and packed together, like earth.

On the top there was irritation. That was ordinary. That was a man who wanted to go to bed.

Under the irritation there was bitterness.

It was very old. It was older than anything Harry had ever felt in a person, older than Hagrid's grief or Filch's sourness or Snape's loathing. It had been there so long that it had a shape, and the shape was aimed, quite precisely, at one person. Not at anybody here. At somebody a long way off, somebody the old man thought about every day without wanting to.

And under the bitterness, very deep, so deep that Harry nearly missed it, there was something else. It was gruff, and it was clumsy, and it did not want to be there at all. It was aimed at the two of them. It was the feeling of a man who does not like children and has never once in his life been able to stand by while somebody hurt one.

It was not going to tell anybody they were here.

Harry was nearly sure of that. He read it again, carefully, all the way down, and he was sure.

And there was one more thing, small and sour and very human, on the top of the bitterness. The old man was used to being wrong about people. He was used to being told he was wrong. He would have liked, very much, just once, to be shown that he was right about something.

Harry let the faces go.

He did it all at once. He had been holding them for so long that letting them go was like putting down two suitcases at the top of a hill, and his knees nearly went. He put a hand on the back of a chair.

The barman looked up.

He looked at Harry. He looked at the black hair, and the glasses, and the face, and the scar. Then he looked at the robes, which were Slytherin green with a snake on them. Then he looked at Harry's height, which was a thirteen-year-old's, and at Evelyn beside him, plain and brown-haired, in the same green. His eyes were very blue. They were bright and sharp and they did not miss anything.

They went back to the scar.

He did not say anything for a long moment.

"Well," he said at last. "That's new."

He put the glass down.

"You're too short," he said. "And you're too young. And you're in the wrong house." He looked at Evelyn. "And you're nobody I've ever seen. And you came out of nowhere at midnight wearing two other children's faces." He folded the cloth. "Sit down before you fall down. I'll get you something to eat. And then you can tell me as much as you like, and I'll decide how much of it I want to hear, which won't be much."

* * *

He gave them bread and a hard yellow cheese and two cups of milk that tasted very strongly of goat, and he sat down on the other side of the table with his arms folded and watched them eat.

He did not ask them anything.

Harry ate three slices of bread and most of the cheese. He had not known he was so hungry. Evelyn ate one slice of bread, slowly, in four pieces, and drank all of her milk, and did not say anything about the taste, and Harry knew from the way she put the cup down that it had been very bad indeed.

"There's a room upstairs," said the old man. "It's got a bed in it. It's not much of a bed. Nobody's slept in it for about ten years except a goat called Mabel, once, when she was poorly. You can have it."

"Thank you," said Evelyn.

"Don't thank me. I haven't decided anything." He looked at Harry. "You're Potter."

"Yes."

"Not the one up at the school."

"No."

"I didn't think so. I've seen the one up at the school. He's taller, and he's got a face like a slapped arse every time anybody mentions the Ministry, and he's in Gryffindor, God help him." He looked at Harry's robes again. "Slytherin. Well. Well, well. Somebody somewhere got a nasty shock."

"Do you want to know where we came from?" said Harry.

"No," said the old man.

Harry looked at him.

"I've lived in this village a long time, boy. I've learned that people who come in at midnight and tell me where they came from are mostly lying, and the ones who aren't lying are mostly worse. You're here. You're hungry. You can't keep that face up much longer, I can see it on you." He nodded at Harry's hands, which were shaking, slightly, on the table. "That's all I need to know tonight."

He stood up.

"Aberforth," he said. "If you're wondering. Aberforth Dumbledore."

Harry went still.

He read him, and the bitterness came up, right up to the top at the sound of his own surname, and settled down again, slowly, like silt in a glass of water. Aimed at one person. A long way off.

"Dumbledore," said Harry.

"Albus is my brother," said Aberforth. "Before you ask. I'll tell you once and then we needn't talk about him." He picked up the plate. "Bed's up the stairs and on the left. Mind the third step, it isn't there."

* * *

They stayed at the Hog's Head for two days before anything happened.

Harry slept. He slept for fourteen hours the first night, in a narrow lumpy bed in a room that smelled faintly of goat, while Evelyn slept on a pile of blankets on the floor, because she said she would rather sleep on the floor than in a bed Mabel had been poorly in. He woke at two in the afternoon and did not know where he was. Then he knew, and lay on his back for a long time looking at the ceiling, and did not hold anything.

He could feel the village.

It was not like the castle. The castle was a roar, three hundred children and a dozen teachers and Umbridge's quiet sweet certainty under all of it. Hogsmeade was small and scattered. A woman in the house behind, worried about her sister. Two men in the street arguing about a cart. Somebody in the Three Broomsticks, at the far end of the high street, who was frightened all the time in a low steady way, and who Harry thought, from the weight of it, might be Madam Rosmerta. A great many goats, very faintly, like voices in another field.

And under him, in the bar, Aberforth.

Aberforth was always there. He did not seem to go out. He wiped glasses and served the few people who came in during the day, who were mostly hooded and mostly did not speak, and in the evening he went out through the back to the goats, and Harry could feel him out there, in the yard, and the bitterness in him went quiet when he was with the goats. Not gone. Quiet. As though it had been told to wait outside.

On the second evening Harry went down and sat at the bar.

He did not have a plan. He had found that he did not need one with Aberforth. Aberforth said what he thought, and what he thought was usually exactly what he felt, which made him the easiest man to read Harry had met since Hagrid.

"Where's the girl?" said Aberforth.

"Asleep. Or reading. She found a book under the bed."

"That'll be the almanac. Nineteen sixty-two. It's under there to stop the leg wobbling." Aberforth poured him something from a jug. It was more goat's milk. "Tell her to put it back after."

"She will."

They sat. Aberforth wiped a glass.

"You can feel things," said Aberforth. "Can't you."

Harry looked at him.

"I watched you come in. You stopped in the door. You stood there like a dog that's heard something. And then you let those faces go, and you'd never have done that unless you'd made up your mind I wasn't going to sell you." He put the glass down. "I've seen it once before. A long time ago. In a girl. She could feel things. Couldn't stop. Feeling everybody, all the time." He picked up another glass. "It didn't do her much good."

"What happened to her?"

"She died," said Aberforth. "She was fourteen." He wiped the glass. "Next question."

Harry did not ask a next question for a while.

He read the old man. The bitterness was there, but it had changed shape slightly, and under it there was a grief that was even older than the bitterness, and had been there before the bitterness, and was what the bitterness had grown on, the way moss grows on a stone.

"You don't like your brother," said Harry.

Aberforth laughed. It was a short hard sound like a stick breaking.

"Does it show?"

"A bit."

"I'll tell you something about my brother, boy," said Aberforth. He put the glass down and leaned on the bar and looked at Harry with his bright blue eyes, which were Albus Dumbledore's eyes and were nothing like them. "Since you're a Potter, and since it'll come in handy, whatever world you crawled out of. My brother loves people. He does. He's not lying about that. He loves people more than most, and he's cleverer than all of them, and he always knows what's for the best." He tapped the bar with one finger. "And he'll use you. He uses everyone he loves, and he loves you, so watch out."

Harry was quiet.

He was thinking about a mirror in a disused classroom, and an old man in a blue dressing gown telling him a kind lie, and the thing under the sorrow that had been turning him over like a stone in its hands. He was thinking about a hospital wing, and a quiet satisfaction, the satisfaction of a man who has seen the last piece go exactly where he meant it to go. He was thinking about a hut on a night in May, and calm.

He had three lines in his head under Dumbledore's name. He had kept them for two years. He had shown them to Evelyn once.

He added a fourth.

*His brother says: he uses everyone he loves.*

"I know," said Harry.

Aberforth looked at him.

"Do you," he said. It was not a question. He looked at Harry for a long time, and the gruff buried thing under the bitterness came up a little way and looked at Harry too. "Yes. I think you probably do."

He picked up the jug.

"I've sent word," he said. "To somebody. About you. Last night."

Harry went very still.

"Not to him," said Aberforth. "Don't look at me like that. I'd sooner feed you to Mabel. To somebody else. Somebody who's got a right to know there's a Potter in my upstairs room, and who won't go running to my brother with it, because he can't stand being told to sit still any more than I can." He poured. "He'll come or he won't. If he comes, it'll be by the back stairs, and it won't be in a hurry, because he's not allowed out. And if he comes, you'll want to be sitting down."

* * *

He came on the third night.

Harry was in the room upstairs. It was after eleven. Evelyn was sitting on her blankets on the floor with the 1962 almanac on her knee, reading the tide tables for Grimsby, because, she said, they were the only thing in it that was not out of date. Harry was at the window. The window looked out over the yard at the back, where the goats were, and a narrow lane, and beyond the lane the dark fields going up towards the forest.

He felt it before he saw it.

He felt it the way he had felt it once before, on a street corner in Little Whinging, at a dead lamp post by a gap between a garage and a fence.

It was a person's feeling.

It was coming up the lane from the fields, low down, fast, and it was enormous. It was loud the way only a very few people Harry had ever met were loud, Hagrid, Mrs Weasley, the whole of the Slytherin stand at a match. It was loud and it was all one thing, coming up the lane, and this time there was no grief in it, and nothing wild. Harry had felt it before only once, in a room with a mirror in it, from a man with glasses and black hair who had stood behind him in the glass.

It was aimed at the window.

"Evelyn," said Harry.

She looked up.

Something came over the wall of the yard. It came over in one long leap and landed among the goats, who did not seem to mind, and it was a dog. It was a very large black dog, thin, shaggy, with eyes that shone in the dark from the light of the window. It looked up.

It looked straight at Harry.

Then it crossed the yard, and Harry heard the back door, and he heard it come up the stairs, and he heard it miss the third step, which was not there, and swear.

Dogs do not swear.

The door opened.

It was a man.

He was tall and thin, much too thin, with a great deal of black hair that had been washed recently and still needed cutting, and a face that had been handsome once and was still handsome, underneath, in a starved, hollow, used-up way. His eyes were grey. They were very bright. He was wearing robes that were much too good for the Hog's Head, and they were covered in dog hair.

He stopped in the doorway.

He looked at Harry, at the window.

Harry knew the face. He had seen it on the television in Privet Drive, and on the front of Stan Shunpike's newspaper, and on a poster on the wall of the post office four nights ago, blinking at him from very far back. Now it was right here, six feet away, in the doorway of a room that smelled of goats, and it was looking at him.

Sirius Black.

Harry did not move.

He had a list in the inside pocket of his robe. It was folded twice. It said: *When he comes, I don't fight him. I read him instead.*

He read him.

And it was love.

It was all love. It came across the room at him like a wave coming up a beach, and it did not stop, and there was so much of it that for a moment Harry could not find anything else. It was the loudest thing he had ever felt apart from Hagrid on a rock, and nearly louder than that. It was so loud that it was nearly painful, the way a light is painful when you have been in the dark, and it was all for him, every bit of it, and none of it was really for him. Most of it belonged to a boy in a tower, two miles away, who was taller and older and in Gryffindor. And it was for a man with glasses and black hair who had been dead for fifteen years. And Harry was standing where both of them should have been, and it had nowhere else to go, so it all came to him.

Under the love, when he could find it, there was recklessness. There was a great deal of it. It was like a horse that has never been broken.

Under that, despair. Grey and flat and very old, a cage of a feeling, and the man had been living in it for a long time and hated it more than anything in the world.

And under the despair, coming up through all of it, right now, at this moment, looking at Harry: delight.

"Merlin," said Sirius Black. "Look at you."

His voice was hoarse. It sounded like a voice that had not been used properly for a long time.

"Look at you," he said again. "You're tiny. You're about twelve. You're a *Slytherin*." He laughed. It was a bark of a laugh, very like a dog's. "Aberforth said. I didn't believe him. I said, Ab, you've finally gone, you've been at the goats too long. Look at you."

He took a step into the room. Harry did not move.

The man stopped.

"Sorry," he said. "Sorry. You don't know me. Of course you don't know me. I'm…"

"I know who you are," said Harry.

His voice came out quiet. It always did, when he was angry. He had not known he was angry until he heard it.

Sirius Black looked at him.

The delight did not go. It stayed exactly where it was. But something came up beside it, quickly, a sharp new attention, the attention of a man who has been hunted for a long time and has just heard a twig snap.

"Do you," he said.

"In my world," said Harry, "you're a murderer."

He said it quite carefully. He had thought, on the window seat, before the dog came over the wall, about how to say it, if he ever said it, and he had decided to say it plainly, because he wanted to see what happened when he did.

"In my world you were my parents' Secret Keeper. You were my father's best friend and you were my godfather, and you gave them to Voldemort inside a week. And then you killed a man called Peter Pettigrew in a street full of Muggles, and twelve Muggles with him, and you stood in the road and laughed. You've been in Azkaban for twelve years. You got out last summer. You came into the castle in February with a knife and stood over Ron Weasley's bed because you thought it was mine." He stopped. "I've been planning to kill you since December."

Evelyn had put down the almanac.

Sirius Black stood in the middle of the room.

He did not say anything for perhaps five seconds. Harry read him the whole time. The love did not go. The delight did not go. But the despair came up, from the bottom, slowly, and it came all the way to the top and spread out over everything, grey and flat, and Harry thought for a moment that the man was going to sit down on the floor.

He did not sit down.

He laughed.

This laugh was nothing like the bark of a moment ago. It was high and thin and dreadful, and it went on too long, and it did not have anything in it that was funny. It was the laugh, Harry thought, of a man in a street full of bodies, and he stood by the window and listened to it and did not move.

It stopped.

"Of course you have," said Sirius Black. "Of course you have. Why wouldn't you? Everybody else has." He wiped his face with the back of his hand. "Merlin. Merlin, I'm sorry. That wasn't for you. That was… you've no idea how funny that is. You can't have. Sit down. Please. Sit down, Harry, and let me tell you about a rat."

* * *

He told it all.

He told it sitting on the end of the narrow bed with his elbows on his knees and his hands hanging, the way Harry had sat in the Room of Requirement, and he did not stop, and Harry did not interrupt him once.

He told him about four boys at Hogwarts. James Potter and Sirius Black and Remus Lupin and Peter Pettigrew. He told him that Remus was a werewolf, and that the three others had spent five years learning to become Animagi so that they could go with him at the full moon and keep him company, and that it had worked. James was a stag. Sirius was the dog. Peter was a rat.

"A rat," said Sirius. "Should've known. Should've known from the start. But he was so…" He moved a hand. "He was ours. He was always just ours. You don't look at your own like that."

He told him that when the Potters went into hiding, everybody had expected Sirius to be their Keeper. Everybody. Including Voldemort. And that Sirius had thought he was being clever.

"I said, use Peter. Nobody'll think of Peter. They'll come for me, and I'll hold out, and they'll never even look at him." He laughed again, very short. "Brilliant. I was very pleased with myself. I thought I was a genius. I was twenty-one."

He told him that he had gone to check on Peter on the night of Hallowe'en, and found his hideout empty, and no sign of a struggle. That he had gone to Godric's Hollow. That he had seen the house.

He did not tell him what he had seen. He stopped, there, and did not go on for a while, and Harry read him, and did not need him to.

He told him about the street.

"I cornered him. Peter. Next day. I'd gone looking. I found him in a street full of Muggles and I had my wand out and I was going to kill him, I'm not going to pretend I wasn't. And he shouted. So everybody could hear. *Lily and James, Sirius, how could you.* And then, before I could do anything, he blew the street apart behind his back, and he cut off his own finger, and he turned into a rat, and he went down the sewer with the rest of them." Sirius looked at his hands. "That's the finger they found. That's all of him they found. His own finger. He cut it off himself. I've thought about that every day for fourteen years. I couldn't have done that. I'd never have thought of it."

"And you laughed," said Harry.

"I laughed." Sirius did not look up. "Twelve dead Muggles and James and Lily gone and the little rat had done me, done me completely, in about four seconds, and I was going to Azkaban for it, and I knew it. Of course I laughed. What else was there to do?"

Harry read him.

It was true.

He read it the way he had read Hagrid in the Three Broomsticks, all the way down, every layer, and it was true. Every word. There was no lie anywhere in it. There was the old despair, and under the despair the old fury, and under the fury, at the very bottom, so deep it had worn a channel in him, there was grief. It was grief for James. It was the oldest, plainest, most worn-smooth grief Harry had ever felt. It was older than Aberforth's. It had been the floor of this man's life for fifteen years.

It was true.

Harry sat on the window seat.

He thought about a list, folded twice, in the inside pocket of his robe. He thought about writing it in blue-black ink at a black stone desk with snow on his shoulders. He thought about the tenth line. *Quirrell did it himself.*

He thought about a big book with brass corners, and a passage he had marked, and Evelyn sitting on her cushion with her face like a shut door saying *I'm not going to be the person who looked it up.*

He thought about the eighteenth of December. Seven weeks. And two days. And then the rest of February, and the beginning of March.

He had spent three months planning, very calmly, very neatly, to find the deepest thing in an innocent man and give it back to him until his heart stopped.

He did not say anything.

He found that his hands were shaking, and he did not try to stop them.

"Which toe?"

It was Evelyn.

She was sitting on her blankets on the floor with the almanac closed on her knee, and she was looking at Sirius, and her face was the same as always.

Sirius looked at her as though he had only just noticed she was there.

"What?"

"The rat," said Evelyn. "He cut off a finger. When he's a rat, which bit's missing? Which paw? Which toe?" She did not change her voice. "If he's still a rat, somebody might have him. Somebody might have a rat with a toe missing. It would help to know which one."

Sirius stared at her.

Then something happened to his face, and the delight came back up through the despair, all at once, like a bubble up through water.

"Who are you?" he said.

"Evelyn Selwyn."

"Selwyn. One of Corvin's?"

"Yes."

"Merlin. I'm sorry for you." He was grinning now. It was a real grin, a young one, and it made his starved face look about twenty. "Front paw. Right front. The middle toe. Clean off at the first joint. I've seen him. I saw him in the paper, in my world, the summer before I got out. Some Ministry man won a prize and had his family photographed in Egypt, and there was the little rat, sitting on his youngest son's shoulder, bold as you like, with his toe missing."

Harry went very still.

"Egypt," he said.

"Egypt. The Weasleys. Arthur Weasley's lot. Big ginger family. Peter's been living as their pet for twelve years." Sirius looked at him. "Why? What is it?"

Harry thought about a bar in the Leaky Cauldron on the last night of August, and a red-haired boy saying very stiffly that they had won a prize, and going red, and going upstairs. He thought about a rat in the boy's top pocket. Old and thin and miserable. Missing a toe.

He thought about a dormitory in Gryffindor Tower, and a man standing over the wrong bed, with a knife.

Not the wrong bed.

The right bed. The bed with the rat on it.

"I've seen it," said Harry. "In my world. In August. Ron Weasley's got it. He had it in his pocket at the Leaky Cauldron." He heard his voice, very quiet. "You didn't come into the tower for me. In my world. You came for the rat."

Sirius looked at him for a long moment.

"I'd imagine I did," he said. "Yes. I'd imagine that's exactly what I did." He rubbed his face with both hands. "Merlin. Me. In your world. Out there on my own with no idea who to trust, and a boy who hates me, and a rat in a tower." He dropped his hands. "Find it, Harry. When you get home. Find the rat. And for God's sake, save my other self some trouble."

* * *

He stayed until two in the morning.

Aberforth brought up a bottle of something that was not goat's milk, and two glasses, and a third glass with goat's milk in it for Harry, and a fourth with goat's milk in it for Evelyn, who looked at it and thanked him and put it on the floor. He did not stay. He looked at Sirius on the end of the bed and Harry on the window seat and said, "Don't be long. You're not supposed to be out. If my brother finds out I'll never hear the end of it," and went back downstairs.

Sirius drank.

He talked about James. He could not stop talking about James. He talked about him the way some people talk about the weather, or the news, because it was the thing that was there. James at eleven on the train. James at fifteen, failing to get anybody to go to Hogsmeade with him. James learning to be a stag.

"Took him three years," said Sirius. "Three years of nothing, and then one night in our fifth year he got it, all at once, at about two in the morning, in the middle of the dormitory. And he was enormous. Antlers out to here. And he couldn't get out of the dormitory, because the door was a door, and he was a stag, and he couldn't turn back, because he'd forgotten how. So he stood there all night in the middle of the floor between the beds with his antlers wedged in the curtains of Frank Longbottom's four-poster, very dignified, absolutely silent, until about six, when he remembered." Sirius was grinning. "Frank slept through the whole thing. Never knew. Woke up and found his bed hangings full of holes and spent a week blaming the house-elves."

Harry laughed.

He did not expect it. It came up out of him all at once, the way it had in a white ward in St Mungo's with a man signing his own get-well cards, and he could not stop it. He thought about a stag in a dormitory with its antlers in the curtains, very dignified, absolutely silent, until about six. He laughed until he had to hold on to the window seat.

Sirius was watching him.

Harry read him and the delight was all the way up, now, at the top of everything, louder than the despair, louder than anything else in him. A man telling a good story did not feel like that.

"That," said Sirius softly. "That's James. That's his laugh. You do it exactly like him."

Harry stopped laughing.

He did not know what to say.

Sirius looked down into his glass.

"He's…" he said. He stopped. "Harry. The other one. Mine. Up at the school." He did not look up. "You've seen him? Aberforth said you'd been up there a week."

"Yes," said Harry. "I've seen him."

"Is he all right?"

Harry did not answer at once.

"I can't get to him," said Sirius. "I'm not allowed out. Dumbledore's orders. I'm stuck in a house I hate, with a house-elf who hates me, and a portrait of my mother screaming at me from behind the curtains in the hall, and he's up there with that woman, with Umbridge, and I can't… I get letters. Sometimes. When it's safe. He doesn't say much." He turned the glass round. "Is he happy? You'd know. You can tell, can't you? Ab said. Is he all right?"

Harry looked at him.

He thought about the tall boy in the corridor outside the library, with his hands in his pockets and his face set, angry at everything, so angry that it had worn a groove in him. He thought about the red-haired boy and the bushy-haired girl walking either side of him, loving him, and the boy not noticing. He thought about a room full of people who trusted him like a staircase, and a stag walking through a wall.

He thought about the cold thing at the bottom of him, in the place where he lived, that was not his.

He read Sirius.

He read him very carefully. The love, enormous, aimed at the window and the tower and the boy in it. The recklessness. The despair, the grey flat cage of it. And under all of it, right now, holding very still, waiting for the answer, a need. It was the simplest thing Harry had ever felt in him. It was the need of a man in a cage for one thing in the world to be all right.

It needed the answer to be yes.

"Yes," said Harry. "He's all right. He's got friends. Two of them. They're always with him. He's teaching a club. Defence. A dozen people. They'd follow him anywhere." He paused. "He's angry. About the Ministry. But he's all right."

Sirius closed his eyes.

Harry read the need go, all at once, the way a held breath goes. Something came up behind it that was so much like relief that Harry could not tell it apart.

"Good," said Sirius. "Good. That's good." He opened his eyes and grinned again, and finished his drink. "Course he is. James's boy. He'd be all right in a cellar."

Harry did not say anything.

He did not know if it was true. He had read every bit of the tall boy that he could reach, and he had read the anger and the love round him and the cold at the bottom, and he did not know whether any of it added up to a boy who was all right, and he had said yes because a man who was going back to a cage needed him to.

He thought that he had done it very well. He thought it was the kindest lie he had ever told.

He was not sure the two things were different.

* * *

Sirius went at two.

He stood up and stretched, and his back cracked, and he looked round the small room with the goat smell and the lumpy bed and the almanac on the floor, and at Evelyn on her blankets, who had not said anything since the toe, and at Harry on the window seat.

"I'll come back," he said. "If Ab'll let me. If I can get out." He hesitated. "You'll be here?"

"I don't know," said Harry. "We're trying to get home."

"Right. Course you are." Sirius looked at him. "If you get there before I come back. If I don't see you." He stopped. Something moved in his face, quickly, and was gone. "Find the rat."

"I will."

"And Harry." Sirius was at the door. "The other me. Out there in your world, on his own, with his knife." He said it lightly. "Go easy on him. He's had a rotten time. And he's an idiot. But he'd die for you, whatever he looks like. I know he would." He grinned. "I would."

He went out.

Harry heard him on the stairs. He heard him miss the third step again, and swear again, more quietly. He heard the back door.

He went to the window.

The yard was dark. The goats were huddled together against the far wall, asleep. And then the back door opened below him, and a dog came out of it.

It was a huge black dog, thin and shaggy, and it crossed the yard without hurrying, between the sleeping goats, to the wall. It stopped at the bottom of the wall. It turned its head and looked up at the window, at Harry, with its eyes catching the light.

It looked at him for a long moment.

Then it went over the wall in one long leap, and down the lane, low and fast, towards the dark fields and the forest, and Harry stood at the window and watched it go, and went on watching the place where it had gone long after there was nothing in the lane at all.

Behind him, Evelyn picked up the almanac again and opened it at the tide tables for Grimsby, and did not read them.

## Chapter 29: The Other Watch

Evelyn showed Aberforth the watch on the Thursday after Sirius came, at the bar, at eleven in the morning, because she had decided that a man who did not want to know anything was the safest person in the world to show it to.

She put it on the bar between them, on a cloth.

"It stopped," she said. "When we came. It won't wind. I want to know who made it."

Aberforth did not pick it up.

Harry was on the next stool. He had been reading Aberforth all morning out of habit, the bitterness and the grief under it and the gruff thing under that, and he was reading him when Evelyn put the watch down, and so he felt it happen.

Aberforth went still.

It was not a large stillness from the outside. He did not move his hands. His face did not change much. He looked down at the small gold watch on the dirty cloth with its ivy-leaf lid, and he did not touch it, and he did not say anything.

Inside, everything stopped.

The bitterness stopped. The irritation stopped. The packed old earth of him, all of it, went quite still, the way a field goes still when a hawk goes over, and then something came up through the stillness that Harry had not felt in him before. It was shock. It was very old shock, older than Harry, much older than Harry's parents, and it was so large and so sudden that Harry thought the old man might sit down. It had not come up in him like that, Harry thought, for fifty years. Perhaps more.

Aberforth reached out one finger and turned the watch over.

He looked at the back of the case. He looked at the tiny mark under the ivy leaves, worn almost smooth, the little triangle with something inside it.

He turned it back.

"Where did you get this?" he said.

His voice was perfectly ordinary. Harry read the shock still going on underneath it, enormous, and the ordinary voice sitting on top of it like a lid on a boiling pan.

"My grandmother gave it to me," said Evelyn. "When I was eleven."

"Your grandmother."

"Isadora Hale."

Aberforth closed his eyes.

He kept them closed for about four seconds. Harry counted, because he knew Evelyn would be counting. When he opened them again the shock had gone down a little way, and in its place there was something that Harry could only have called recognition, and it was bitter, very bitter, and it was not aimed at anybody in the room.

"Who made it?" said Evelyn.

"I'm not going to tell you that."

"You know."

"I know," said Aberforth. "I've seen work like it once in my life, and I've seen that mark more than I'd ever want to. I know whose hand made that, girl, and I'm not going to tell you."

"Why not?"

"Because it's not mine to tell." He pushed the watch back across the cloth towards her with one finger, the way you might push a coin back to somebody who has offered too much. "Ask whoever gave it to you."

"She's dead," said Evelyn.

Aberforth looked at her.

"In February," said Evelyn. "In my world. In her sleep. In June, in yours. I found it in the *Prophet*." Her voice did not change at all. "There isn't anybody to ask. That's why I'm asking you."

Harry read him.

The bitterness came back up, slowly, and with it, just under it, the clumsy gruff thing that did not want to be there. It was looking at Evelyn. It was sorry. It was very sorry.

"I'm sorry," said Aberforth.

"Thank you."

"I'm still not going to tell you."

"No," said Evelyn. "I didn't think you would." She picked up the watch and closed it and held it in her hand. "Then tell me what it is. You can tell me that. It isn't anybody's secret what a thing is."

Aberforth looked at her for a long time.

"A Seer made it," he said at last. "That's what it is. It's a Seer's piece. There's nothing else like it. Most people who see the future see it in fits and starts, in smoke, in tea leaves, in their sleep, and they can't do anything with it but shout. A few, a very few, see it plainly. And one or two of those, once in a hundred years, learn to put what they see into a thing. A ring. A glass. A watch." He nodded at her hand. "That's a watch that knows where the next hour is. Not the one after this. The one beside it."

"Beside it," said Evelyn.

"There's more than one way things could have gone. Every time. You know that, I expect, you're a clever girl. That watch knows the nearest. And if you wind it the wrong way, it takes you there." He looked at Harry. "As you've found out."

"How do we get back?" said Harry.

Aberforth was quiet for a while. He picked up a glass and did not wipe it.

"It'll have a twin," he said. "Here. A thing like that, made by a hand like that, would have been made more than once. Wherever the maker was, he made it again. Same hand, same watch, same girl to give it to." He put the glass down. "To go home, you'd need the twin from this side. Wound forwards. By somebody of the same blood as the girl it was made for. In a place where time is held still."

"What's a place where time is held still?" said Evelyn.

"There aren't many." Aberforth did not look at them. "There's one I know of. In London. Under the Ministry. There's a part of it nobody talks about, where they keep things nobody understands, and in it there's a room full of clocks. I've never been in it. My brother has." He made a small sour noise. "My brother's been everywhere."

"The Department of Mysteries," said Evelyn.

Aberforth looked at her sharply.

"My father sits on the Wizengamot," said Evelyn. "He mentions it. He doesn't say what's in it. He says it the way people say *the cellar*, when there's something in the cellar."

"Then your father's got more sense than I'd have credited a Selwyn with," said Aberforth. He picked up his cloth. "Twin. Forwards. Her blood. A room full of clocks under London." He began, at last, to wipe the glass. "That's all I know. That's all I'm going to say. And you don't want to go anywhere near that building this summer, either of you. There's things moving there you've no idea about."

He turned away.

Harry read him all the way to the end of the bar. The shock had gone down. It had not gone away. It was sitting in him now, under the bitterness, very large and very quiet, with something new beside it, and the new thing was fear. It was not fear for himself.

It was aimed at the watch.

* * *

"Same blood," said Evelyn, upstairs, on her blankets, with her notebook. "Same blood as the girl it was made for. That's my grandmother. Or my mother. Or me." She wrote it down. "Or her."

"The other Evelyn."

"She's got the twin. She winds it every morning. Twenty turns. I've watched her." Evelyn closed the notebook. "She's of the blood. She's got the watch. That's two of the three. The third's a room under London that we can't get into."

"One thing at a time," said Harry.

"That's what my grandmother used to say." Evelyn looked at the closed notebook on her knee. "She used to say it in French, so Mother couldn't follow."

* * *

They went back into the castle on the Saturday, through Honeydukes and the long passage, with Harry holding the two faces.

He was better at it now. He had slept for most of a week in the room over the bar, and eaten, and the doors he held were still doors and the wind against them was still wind, but his shoulder against them was stronger. He could hold the two faces for a day. He thought that he could probably hold them for two, if he had to, and then he thought that he did not want to find out.

They had a plan. It was Evelyn's plan. It was very simple.

"I'm going to talk to her," she had said. "On my own. Somewhere nobody comes. And you're not going to be there."

"I should be there."

"You shouldn't. You'll read her. She'll know." Evelyn had looked at him. "She's me, Potter. She'll have had the lessons. Every morning from five. She'll be like me. You won't get anything from her, and your face will do the thing it does when you don't get anything, and she'll see it, and she'll want to know what you are." She had folded her arms. "And your face won't work on her either. If she's me. Nothing you put on her will take. She'll see you."

Harry had not thought of that.

He thought about it now, coming up through the trapdoor under the one-eyed witch, with the corridor dark and empty and the castle quiet round him. Somewhere under the lake, in the dungeons, in a sixth-year dormitory, there was a girl he could not read, and could not fool, and had never met.

There were two of them now.

He did not know what he felt about that.

* * *

The Inquisitorial Squad caught him on the Monday, outside the Charms corridor, at twenty past four.

He was on his own. Evelyn was in the library, following the other Evelyn at a distance, waiting for an empty room. Harry had gone to look at the Map in a disused bathroom on the third floor and had come out at the wrong moment, and there were three of them, coming round the corner: two Slytherin fifth-years he did not know, and Draco Malfoy.

"You," said Malfoy.

Harry kept walking.

"You. Hufflepuff. Stop."

Harry stopped.

He read them. The two fifth-years were bored and slightly hopeful, the way people are hopeful when they think they might be about to be allowed to hurt somebody. Malfoy was pleased. Malfoy was very pleased. He had a list in his hand, and he was looking at Harry's face, the round mousy face with the ears that stuck out, and he was matching it against something.

"Second-year," said Malfoy. "Hufflepuff. Ears. You're one of them, aren't you. The two that've been missing. Cuthbert." He smiled. "We've been looking for you for a fortnight. Professor Umbridge is going to be *delighted*."

Harry thought about running.

He thought about the Cloak in his bag, and the bathroom behind him, and the three of them, and he read Malfoy and found that Malfoy wanted him to run, very badly, because it would be more fun.

He did not run.

"Where's the other one?" said one of the fifth-years. "The girl."

"Don't know," said Harry.

"He doesn't know," said Malfoy. "Of course he doesn't. Come on, Cuthbert. Headmistress's office. Let's see what you know when she's asked you nicely."

* * *

The headmistress's office was not Dumbledore's office.

Harry did not know what Dumbledore's office had looked like in this world, but he had been in it at home, the night of the fourth of May, wet and filthy with a sword in his hand and Mrs Weasley's arms round him. He remembered the silver instruments and the portraits of old headmasters asleep in their frames and the phoenix on its perch.

None of it was there.

Or it was there, and he could not see it. The office was round, the same as before, and the walls were the same walls, but they had been covered. Every inch of them that he could see was covered with lace, and pink, and plates. Ornamental plates. There were dozens of them, hung in rows, and on each plate there was a kitten. The kittens moved. They frolicked. They played with balls of wool, and pounced on each other, and looked out at the room with large round eyes.

The portraits were behind curtains. The phoenix's perch was empty.

Umbridge was behind the desk.

She was writing, with a short black quill, and she did not look up when Malfoy brought him in, and she let them stand there for about a minute, and Harry read her the whole time.

It was the same as at the staff table. Quiet. Pleased. Certain. Under the certainty, sweetly, the thing that enjoyed being the one who dealt with people. It was enjoying this. It was enjoying the minute.

She looked up.

"Well," she said. She had a soft, high, girlish voice, which went very badly with the rest of her. "Well, well. Mr Malfoy. What have we here?"

"One of the missing second-years, Professor. Hufflepuff. Cuthbert, he says."

"Cuthbert." Umbridge smiled at Harry. It was a wide, wet smile, with nothing in it, and Harry read her while she did it and found that she was looking forward to the next ten minutes more than she had looked forward to anything all week. "Do sit down, dear."

Harry sat down.

"There is no Cuthbert," said Umbridge, "in the Hufflepuff second year. There is no Cuthbert in Hufflepuff. There is no Cuthbert at Hogwarts. I have looked." She put down her quill. "And so I find myself wondering, dear, who exactly you might be, and what you are doing in my school."

Harry looked at her.

He thought about saying something. He thought about saying something very true and very clever, the way he had at the Leaky Cauldron with Fudge, and then he looked at the kittens, and at the curtained portraits, and at the empty perch, and at the wide wet smile, and he read the thing under the certainty, sweetly looking forward, and he thought that there was nothing true or clever that would make any difference to her at all.

So he did something else.

He had never done it to anybody who was looking straight at him. He had done coins on tables, and faces on himself and Evelyn. He had never set a thing in front of somebody who did not know it was coming, while she watched him, and held it.

He thought about a cat.

He thought about it very carefully. A very large cat, a tomcat, ginger, old and scarred and battle-torn, the sort of cat that sits on the wall at the back of the chip shop in Little Whinging and looks at you as though you owe it money. One ear half gone. A belly that swung. He held it in his head until he could see every whisker.

He set it on the desk.

He set it only for her. Not for Malfoy, or the two fifth-years by the door. Only for the woman in pink, the way he would have set a coin on a table for one person. He put it on the desk at her elbow, sitting on her papers, enormous and ginger and very still, looking at her.

Umbridge's eyes went to it.

She stopped smiling.

Harry read her. There was no fear in it. It was something more like outrage. It went straight up, through the pleasure and the certainty, all at once, and it was outrage that a thing should be there, on her desk, on her papers, which had not been given permission to be there.

"*What*," said Umbridge, in a much less girlish voice, "is *that*?"

Malfoy looked at the desk. He looked at Umbridge. He did not see anything, because there was nothing to see.

"Professor?"

The cat stood up.

Harry made it stand up. He made it stretch, very slowly, all along its scarred ginger back, the way old cats do, and he made it turn round once on her papers, and walk to the edge of the desk, and look up at the wall.

At the plates.

"Get down," said Umbridge. "Get *down*, you filthy creature."

The cat jumped.

It went up off the desk in one heavy leap and landed on the lowest row of plates, and Harry made her hear it, the clatter, and made her see the plate swing. The kitten on the plate screamed silently and ran off the edge of the china.

"*No*," said Umbridge.

She was on her feet. She had her wand out.

The cat walked along the row of plates. It walked very slowly, with great dignity, and as it passed each plate it put out one paw, quite casually, and knocked it. Each plate swung. Each kitten fled. And Umbridge came round the end of her desk with her wand up and her face going a dark, mottled pink, and she pointed her wand at the cat, and the cat looked at her over its shoulder, and Harry made it yawn.

"*Professor Umbridge?*" said Malfoy.

Umbridge did not hear him. She fired a spell at the wall. It went through the place where the cat was and hit a plate, a real plate, which cracked across the middle, and the kitten in it went white with fright and hid behind its own ball of wool.

The cat was not there any more.

It was on top of the curtained portraits, on the rail. It was washing itself.

"Get it," said Umbridge, in a high, terrible voice. "Get it, get it, Draco, *get that animal out of my office*."

Malfoy looked at the curtain rail.

He looked at it very hard. Harry read him. Malfoy could see nothing on the curtain rail but curtain rail. He was confused. Under the confusion he was frightened, a little, because a headmistress was shrieking at a curtain rail, and under that, a long way down, and very quietly, a part of Malfoy that did not like Umbridge any more than Harry did was beginning, very slightly, to enjoy itself.

"Professor," said Malfoy carefully. "There isn't…"

"*Get it!*"

Malfoy pointed his wand at the curtain rail and said something. The curtain came down. Behind it, in a frame, an old wizard with a long white beard woke up and said, "Good heavens, what's all this," and Umbridge screamed at him too.

Harry stood up.

Nobody was looking at him. Nobody in the room was looking at anything but the curtain rail and the plates and the headmistress, purple in the face, firing spells at a wall. He walked to the door. The two fifth-years by the door were staring at Umbridge with their mouths open. He walked between them. He opened the door, and stepped out onto the moving staircase, and closed it behind him, and as he went down he let the cat go.

He held the face. He let the cat go.

He made it go very slowly. He made it walk to the window, and sit on the sill, and look at Umbridge for a long moment, with great contempt, the way the cats on the wall behind the chip shop look at everybody. And then he took it away, the way you take a coin off a table, and through the door, faintly, as the staircase turned, he heard her say, in a voice like a kettle about to go, "Where did it *go*?"

He went down the stairs.

He was smiling. He could feel it. He could not stop.

He thought about Umbridge's face, mottled purple, firing curses at her own plates, and he thought about a kitten going white with fright behind its ball of wool, and he thought about a woman in a pink office who enjoyed dealing with people, being dealt with, for once, by somebody she could not see.

He enjoyed it.

He enjoyed it all the way down the staircase and all the way along the corridor and round the corner, very much, and he did not try to stop enjoying it, and he did not think, until much later, that he had done to her more or less exactly what she enjoyed doing to everybody else.

* * *

Evelyn found her in an empty classroom on the fifth floor, at ten past five on the Tuesday, alone.

She had followed her there. She had followed her from the library, at a distance, as a Hufflepuff second-year with freckles, and she had watched her go in and close the door, and she had waited outside in the corridor for four minutes to see whether anybody else came.

Nobody came.

Nobody ever would, Evelyn thought. That was why she had chosen it.

She went in.

The other Evelyn was at a desk by the window with a book. No schoolbook: a small, battered paperback with a green spine, and Evelyn knew it from across the room before she could read the title, because she had the same copy in the false bottom of her trunk at home. Margery Allingham. *The Tiger in the Smoke.* Bought from Mr Ainsworth on Corve Street for sixty pence.

The other Evelyn looked up.

She looked at the door, and at the person in it, and Evelyn waited, because this was the question, and she had been waiting since Saturday to find out the answer.

The other Evelyn looked straight at her.

She did not look at freckles, or fair hair, or a pointed chin, or Hufflepuff robes. Evelyn watched her eyes and they did not stop on any of those things. They went to her face, her real face, her plain brown hair, her Slytherin badge, and they stayed there, and the other Evelyn's own face did not change at all, except that very slowly, over about three seconds, it went white.

"Close the door," said the other Evelyn.

Evelyn closed the door.

They looked at each other.

"I wondered," said the other Evelyn, "whether it was the light."

"It isn't the light."

"No." The other Evelyn put the book face down on the desk. She did it very carefully, square to the edge. "I saw you in the Great Hall on the twenty-ninth. At the Hufflepuff table. Everyone else saw a little fair girl. I saw you. I thought it was the light. Then I saw you in the corridor outside Charms, and the library, and on the stairs, and you were always you." She folded her hands. "I thought I was going mad. I decided I wasn't. I don't."

"No," said Evelyn. "We don't."

The other Evelyn looked at her for a long moment.

"What do you want?" she said.

Evelyn had thought about how to say it. She had thought about it for four days. She had decided, in the end, to say it the way she would have wanted it said to her, which was in order, precisely, all at once.

So she did.

She told her about the watch. About the morning lessons, and the breakfast, and twenty turns. About Potter, and a study under the Chamber, and a lamp that lit for him and not for her. About February, and the low chair, and *never wind it backwards*. About three turns and one tick. About the skeleton, and the dust, and the date in a pink frame. About Aberforth Dumbledore and a Seer's piece and a twin and a room full of clocks under London.

She did not tell her about Isadora's last question. She did not tell her where Potter stood.

The other Evelyn listened to all of it without moving.

When it was finished she sat for a while with her hands folded on the desk.

"You could be lying," she said.

"I could be."

"You could be anybody. Polyjuice. A Metamorphmagus. Somebody who wants the watch." The other Evelyn's voice was perfectly level. "I'd like to test you."

"Go on."

"What did Grandmother say, the first time she gave it to you?"

"*Wind it every morning.*"

"What else?"

"Nothing else. She didn't say anything else until December, this year. In my world."

The other Evelyn's hands tightened very slightly on each other.

"What did Mr Pelham say about Cicero?"

"That he was a bore." Evelyn did not hesitate. "And Catullus was a scandal, and Tacitus was the only one worth reading. And then he made me read Cicero."

"How many yews in the walk?"

"A hundred and twelve each side. Great-great-grandfather counted them in eighteen sixty-one. I counted them in nineteen eighty-seven. I got a hundred and eleven on the left the first time and had to go back."

The other Evelyn closed her eyes.

"What's in the false bottom of the trunk?"

"Allingham. Sayers. Tey. Marsh. *The Nine Tailors*, first edition, nineteen thirty-four, the jacket mended with paper tape. *Bells are also a kind of clock.*" Evelyn stopped. "Did she give you that one?"

"Yes."

"When?"

"The Christmas I stayed at school. In my third year." The other Evelyn opened her eyes. "I stayed because the library was empty. And Lucan was trying. And because of Runes."

"That wasn't the reason."

"No," said the other Evelyn. "It wasn't."

They did not ask each other what the reason was.

Evelyn thought that she knew what hers had been, now. She thought that it had been sitting in a common room at home, at Christmas, with Potter not twenty feet away, playing the Heir. She did not know what the other Evelyn's had been. She thought that perhaps the other Evelyn did not know either. She thought that perhaps there had not been one, and that the other Evelyn had stayed at school over Christmas in her second year for a reason she could not put into words, and had found when she got there that there was nobody in the castle who would have noticed if she had gone home.

"I believe you," said the other Evelyn.

"Thank you."

"I'm not going to help you."

Evelyn did not say anything.

"I've got no reason to," said the other Evelyn. She said it quite reasonably. "You're a stranger. You've got my face and you've got my life, or a version of it, and you've got somebody. You've got a boy who reads people and a lamp that lights for him and a study under the Chamber and an adventure. And you want me to go to London with you, to a building under the Ministry that nobody's allowed into, and wind my watch forwards in a room full of clocks, so that you can go home." She put her hand flat on the paperback. "And then I won't have it any more. Will I? The old man said. *Same blood, forwards, in a room where time is held.* He didn't say what happens to the watch."

"I don't know what happens to the watch."

"No. Neither do I." The other Evelyn looked at her. "It's the only thing she gave me. The only thing that was mine. The only thing anybody's ever given me that was just for me and nobody else. I wind it every morning. It's the only time all day anybody's thinking about me, even if it's only me." She stood up. She picked up *The Tiger in the Smoke* and put it in her bag. "I'm sorry. I really am. I know what it is to be stuck somewhere. I'm not going to help you."

She went to the door.

She stopped in it.

"You should tell him," she said, without turning round, "that his face doesn't work on me either. In case he hasn't worked it out. The little fair girl. I can see straight through it. If there's anybody else in this castle who's been taught what I've been taught, they'll see straight through it too."

She went out.

Evelyn sat down at the desk by the window where the other Evelyn had been sitting.

She sat there for a long time.

She did not write anything down.

* * *

It was Pansy Parkinson who changed it.

Evelyn did not see it coming. Potter would have. Potter would have felt it from the end of the corridor. But Potter was at the other end of the castle, hiding from the Inquisitorial Squad in a broom cupboard on the sixth floor because of something to do with a cat that he had not yet explained, and Evelyn was on her own, on the Thursday, coming down the stairs to the dungeons behind the other Evelyn at a careful distance, and she only saw it when it was already happening.

There were four of them. Pansy and three other fifth-year girls. They were at the bottom of the stairs, by the corner where the dungeon corridor turned, and the other Evelyn had to go past them to get to the common room.

Pansy put out her foot.

The other Evelyn stepped over it. She did not stop. She did not look at it.

"Oh, sorry," said Pansy. "I didn't see you. I never do." The other girls laughed. "What's your name again? I've been in the same house as you for five years and I've honestly never known. Selwyn, isn't it? Lucan Selwyn's sister? Isn't it funny, he was so *nice*, and so good-looking, and everyone knew who he was."

The other Evelyn kept walking.

"I heard your grandmother died," said Pansy, to her back. "Two years ago. Didn't you go home for the funeral? Somebody said you went home for the funeral and nobody noticed you'd gone for a week."

The other Evelyn stopped.

She did not turn round. She stood quite still in the dungeon corridor with her back to them and her bag on her shoulder and her hands at her sides.

Evelyn knew what she was doing. She was closing the door. Ten to seven, every morning since she was five. *Close the door, Evelyn. Again.* She was standing in the corridor with Pansy Parkinson laughing at her back, and she was closing the door.

Evelyn came down the last three stairs.

She did not decide to. She thought about it afterwards and she could not remember deciding. She was simply at the bottom of the stairs, a small fair freckled Hufflepuff second-year as far as anybody but the girl at the end of the corridor could tell, and she was standing in front of Pansy Parkinson, looking up at her.

"Parkinson," she said.

Pansy looked down at her.

"Who are you?"

"Nobody," said Evelyn. "You've got ink on your left wrist."

Pansy's hand went behind her back.

It went very fast. Too fast. The other girls looked at it.

"I haven't," said Pansy.

"You have. On the inside. You tried to wash it off this morning, with soap, but it was the good ink, the kind from Scrivenshaft's that's charmed not to run, and soap won't touch it. You need lemon juice. There's a faint ring of it left." Evelyn did not change her voice at all. "It's two letters. With a shape round them."

Pansy had gone very red.

"You don't know what you're talking about."

"*D. M.*," said Evelyn. "And a heart. It's not a very good heart. One side's bigger than the other. You did it in Potions, I expect, because the lines are wobbly, the way they go when you're writing under a desk." She looked at the other three girls. "You can see it from here if she holds her arm up."

Nobody said anything.

The three fifth-year girls were looking at Pansy's hand, behind her back. One of them had begun, very slightly, to grin.

"Lemon juice," said Evelyn again. "Before Malfoy sees it. He comes down these stairs at twenty to six, every day, on his way back from the Squad. He'll be here in four minutes."

Pansy looked at her for one second longer.

Then she turned round and went down the dungeon corridor very fast, with her hand still behind her back, and the three other girls went after her, and the one who had been grinning was laughing out loud by the time they reached the stone wall.

Evelyn stood at the bottom of the stairs.

The other Evelyn had turned round.

She was looking at Evelyn, the real Evelyn, through the little fair freckled girl that was not there. She looked for a long time. Her face was quite still. Her face was Evelyn's face, two years older, and Evelyn could not read it either, and she found that she did not need to.

Neither of them said anything.

Then the other Evelyn turned round again, and went on down the corridor, and through the wall.

* * *

She came to the Hog's Head that night.

Harry felt the door go downstairs at eleven. He did not feel anything else. Nobody had come into the bar; the bar was empty except for Aberforth. And then he heard Aberforth say, "We're shut," and somebody answer, and he could not hear what, and he could not feel who, and he knew.

He looked at Evelyn.

She had already put the almanac down.

There were footsteps on the stairs. They missed the third step. They did not swear. They paused, and stepped over the gap, and came on up, and the door of the room opened.

The other Evelyn stood in it.

She was in her school robes. She had come down through the passage, Harry thought, or out by the gates, past the Dementors that were not there any more in this world. She had her bag on her shoulder. She looked at the room, the lumpy bed and the blankets and the almanac, and she looked at Harry by the window, with his own face on, which she could see, and then she looked at Evelyn.

Harry did not try to read her.

He did not need to try. There was nothing there. There was the same nothing there was in Evelyn, the same smooth complete wall, and it was so exactly the same that for a moment, sitting on the window seat in the goat-smelling room above the bar, he could not tell which of the two silences was which.

He could tell. He always could. He did not know how.

"I watched you," said the other Evelyn. She was speaking to Evelyn. "Both of you. For a week. Since the Great Hall. I watched you in the library, and the corridors, and at the Hufflepuff table pretending to eat."

"I know," said Evelyn. "I watched you too."

"I know you did."

The other Evelyn came a step into the room.

"He stands next to you," she said. "Always. Even when there's room somewhere else. On your left."

Evelyn did not say anything.

"I counted," said the other Evelyn. "I couldn't help it."

"No," said Evelyn. "We can't."

The other Evelyn looked at Harry, at the window, and then back at Evelyn. Her face did not change. Her voice did not change. She said the next thing very quietly, and very precisely, the way she said everything, the way Evelyn said everything, as though it were a fact she was reporting about the weather.

"How long have you been friends?"

Evelyn looked at Harry.

She looked at him for a moment. It was only a moment. And then she looked back at the other girl in the doorway, and said:

"Three years. Nearly."

The other Evelyn nodded slowly, as though that were the figure she had expected, and it was the right one.

"Nobody has ever looked for me," she said.

She said it the way Evelyn had said *two*.

Then she took her hand out of her cardigan pocket. There was a thin gold chain wound round her fingers, and at the end of it, small and gold, with ivy leaves on the lid worn smooth in the middle, there was a watch, ticking.

"I'll come," she said.
